page: Microsoft Azure E64_v5 is a memory-optimized virtual machine instance powered by a 2.8 GHz Intel Xeon 8370C processor built on the x86_64 architecture. The configuration supplies 64 dedicated vCPUs distributed across 32 physical cores with hyperthreading enabled, supported by 105 MB of L3 cache. It incorporates 512.0 GB of system memory, establishing an 8.0 GB per core ratio designed for memory-intensive computations without dedicated GPU hardware.

Benchmark measurements indicate strong multi-threaded and memory subsystem performance. The system registered 62127.65 in stress-ng multi-core tests and 16157.0 in Geekbench multi-core evaluation, alongside strong memory bandwidth achieving 286.33 GB/sec on large-block uncached reads. In contrast, single-threaded processing remains average, with stress-ng single-core reaching 1899.08 and Geekbench single-core at 1638.0. Large-scale transformer inferencing on 70B parameter models demonstrates constrained execution at 2.74 tokens per second during generation tasks.

Resource density supports cost-efficient consolidation of heavy concurrent memory footprints onto a single host. The platform is well matched for in-memory databases, large relational database operations, Clang-based software compilation, distributed caching, and static web serving, while single-thread-constrained processes and accelerated machine learning run less efficiently.
description: Microsoft Azure E64_v5 is a memory-optimized virtual machine featuring 64 dedicated vCPUs and 32 physical cores running on a 2.8 GHz Intel Xeon 8370C processor with x86_64 architecture and a 105 MB L3 cache. Provisioned with 512.0 GB of RAM, the instance delivers an 8.0 GB per core memory profile. Empirical benchmarks reveal strong multi-core throughput and memory access speeds, registering 62127.65 in stress-ng multi-core testing and 286.33 GB/sec in large-block read operations. Parallel execution areas such as Clang compilation, database transaction benchmarks, and static web throughput score within the top tier. Conversely, single-core benchmarks and large-scale language model inference show average to weak results due to lack of specialized accelerator hardware. This instance profile suits enterprise relational databases, large in-memory caches, software compilation systems, and high-concurrency analytical data processing.
